title: Argleton: a correctness suite for geospatial systems
description:
Argleton measures how often a geospatial system answers confidently and wrongly.

Each probe has a right answer known by construction — derived on paper, never measured from a reference implementation — and a typical wrong answer that looks entirely plausible. Every trap ships with a defect-free twin, so a system cannot score well by refusing to answer: the suite reports a silent-error rate alongside a completion rate on the twins, and a refusal counts as neither a pass nor a silent error.

The name is the phantom settlement Google Maps showed for two years near Aughton: an empty field for which the map offered photographs of houses, restaurants and a hospital. Well-formed data, valid against its schema, rendered with confidence, entirely false, and crashing nothing. That is the class of error this suite measures.

Published from an organisation separate from the system it was extracted from, and that relationship is stated in the repository rather than hidden — an evaluation living inside the thing it evaluates can be dismissed in one line.
